flawed_step: The natural proof tries to rebuild G from L(G) by treating each maximal clique in L(G) as the set of edges at one vertex of G. That step fails: a triangle in L(G) can come from three edges that meet at one vertex (a star K_{1,3}) or from three edges that form a triangle (K3). Nothing in L(G) tells these cases apart. This is exactly the exception in Whitney's theorem.
counterexample: G1 = K3 with vertices a, b, c and edges ab, bc, ca. G2 = K_{1,3} with center x, leaves p, q, r and edges xp, xq, xr. Both graphs are connected, finite and simple. L(G1): each pair of edges shares an endpoint (ab and bc share b, bc and ca share c, ab and ca share a), so L(G1) = K3. L(G2): each pair of edges shares x, so L(G2) = K3. The line graphs are isomorphic. But G1 has 3 vertices and G2 has 4 (and the degree sequences are (2,2,2) and (3,1,1,1)), so G1 and G2 are not isomorphic.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. K3 and K_{1,3} are both connected and both have K3 as their line graph, yet they are not isomorphic. Whitney's theorem shows this is the only exception among connected graphs.
